title: Basic Fabrication Steps
intro: The building blocks of every CMOS flow: substrates, lithography, oxidation, ion implantation, deposition and etching (Razavi, Sections 18.1 to 18.6).

blocks.text: A bar of resistivity $\rho$, length $L$, width $W$ and thickness $t$ has $R = \rho L/(Wt)$. In a process $\rho$ and $t$ are fixed, so they are combined into one number:
in ohms per square: a square of any size has resistance $R_□$, and a line $L/W = 10$ squares long has $10R_□$.

The substrate must be a single crystal with very few defects (dislocations, unwanted impurities) and the right doping. In the Czochralski method a rotating seed crystal is dipped into doped molten silicon and slowly drawn out, growing a cylindrical ingot that is sliced into wafers (now 300 mm in diameter), then polished and etched to remove slicing damage. Typical CMOS wafers have 0.05 to 0.1 Ω·cm resistivity and start 0.5 to 1 mm thick.

The layout is split into layers, and each layer is written by an electron beam onto a glass mask. The wafer is coated with photoresist, the mask pattern is projected onto it with ultraviolet light, and the resist is developed so only the wanted regions of silicon are exposed for the next step. Each layer therefore costs one mask and three steps (coat, expose, develop). A negative resist hardens where light hits; a positive resist hardens where it does not; processes use both.

blocks.alt: Four panels: a wafer coated with resist; light passing through a mask with an opaque square onto the resist; after development a window in the resist above the silicon; ions implanted through the window.
blocks.caption: One lithography sequence.

blocks.text: Masks cost tens of thousands of dollars each and lithography is slow and precise. Early CMOS needed about seven masks, modern processes about 30; cost per chip still fell because transistor density and wafer size kept rising. The smallest printable feature is often estimated as $k_1\lambda/\mathrm{NA}$ for wavelength $\lambda$ and numerical aperture NA.

Silicon grows a uniform, low-stress oxide when heated near 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere, which makes gate oxides only a few atomic layers thick possible. Thick field oxide between devices supports interconnect. The gate oxide is the most critical step: $t_{ox}$ sets current drive and reliability, so it must be uniform to a few percent across the wafer (a few ångströms between devices 20 cm apart), which needs slow growth; the cleanliness of the interface sets mobility and noise.

Dopant ions are accelerated in a focused beam into the exposed silicon. Beam intensity and time set the dose; energy sets the depth. A high-energy implant peaks below the surface (a retrograde profile), which for an n-well gives low resistance at the bottom (less latch-up) and light doping at the top (less PMOS junction capacitance).

items: Channel-stop (field) implant: the field oxide with an interconnect over it and two neighbouring diffusions is a parasitic thick-oxide MOSFET; implanting under the field oxide raises its threshold so it cannot turn on.

Annealing: implantation wrecks the lattice, so the wafer is heated (about 1000 °C for 15 to 30 minutes) to repair it. Dopants also diffuse, which causes the lateral diffusion of sources and drains under the gate, so annealing is done once after all implants.
Channeling: ions aligned with a crystal axis travel deep; tilting the beam or wafer by 7 to 9° avoids it. The tilt makes structures asymmetric, which matters for matching (see the layout chapter).

blocks.text: Polysilicon, dielectrics and metals are deposited, typically by chemical vapour deposition (a gas reacts in a furnace to form the film), at low pressure for uniformity. Etching removes material: wet etching in a liquid (low precision), plasma etching (high precision) and reactive ion etching; deep, narrow contact holes need the precise kinds.

blocks.text: 193 nm light, numerical aperture 1.35 (immersion), $k_1 = 0.3$: what is the smallest printable half-pitch?

blocks.title: Counting squares
blocks.text: A poly line has $R_□ = 25\ \Omega/□$, width 0.2 µm and length 10 µm. What is its resistance? What width gives 250 Ω for the same length?

blocks.title: Untilted implant
blocks.text: A threshold-adjust implant (which raises the threshold) is done without tilt, so the ions channel deep into the silicon. Is the threshold higher or lower than intended?
solution: Lower: the dopants end up deeper than planned, so fewer sit near the surface where they set the threshold.
